title: The Centrality of the Cross: Substitutionary Atonement as the Heart of the Message
seoTitle: The Centrality of the Cross | Charles Spurgeon
description: Discover how substitutionary atonement was the absolute center of gravity and the heart of the message for Charles Spurgeon

content.text: The Foundation of the Tabernacle Pulpit

When Charles Haddon Spurgeon inaugurated the massive Metropolitan Tabernacle in 1861, he made a definitive and historic declaration regarding the theological foundation of his future ministry there. Standing before his vast congregation, he proposed that as long as the platform stood and the house was frequented by worshippers, the central theme of his ministry would be "the person of Jesus Christ". While he never hesitated to embrace the titles of Calvinist or Baptist, he famously summarized his ultimate creed by simply stating: "It is Jesus Christ". For Spurgeon, the cross was not merely a doctrine among many; it was the absolute center of gravity for all biblical revelation and Christian experience. His preaching was intensely Christocentric, driven by a burning passion to exalt the incarnate Word of God in every message.

Spurgeon's profound emphasis on the cross was deeply rooted in his Puritan theological heritage. According to church historian Mark Hopkins, Spurgeon cherished the transcendent holiness of God and recognized the vast, terrifying gulf that human sinfulness had created between the Creator and His creatures. The substitutionary atonement of Jesus Christ was the glorious, divine, and only bridge across this impassable abyss. Spurgeon proclaimed that because of this completed substitutionary work, no human merit was needed or accepted; men simply had to accept by faith what Christ had already perfectly accomplished on their behalf. The wrath of God was satisfied, and divine justice was fulfilled entirely through the blood of the Savior, who offered Himself as a sacrifice once and for all.

To the aspiring ministers in his Pastors' College, the "Prince of Preachers" was incredibly emphatic regarding their homiletical priorities: "Preach Christ, always and evermore. He is the whole gospel". He solemnly warned his students against being diverted by philosophy, metaphysics, or even systematic theology and eschatological speculations, if such intellectual pursuits meant withdrawing their focus from glorying in the cross of Christ. Instead, he instructed them that the simple, unadorned gospel—man's fall, the absolute necessity of a new birth, forgiveness through a substitutionary atonement, and salvation as the result of faith—were to be their "battle-ax and weapons of war". This focused, aggressive proclamation of the cross was, in his view, the only genuine antidote to the creeping theological liberalism of his day.

This rigorous theology of substitutionary atonement was never a dry, academic exercise for Spurgeon; rather, it was the necessary fuel for urgent, tender, and passionate evangelism. Because he firmly believed that Christ had literally borne the punishment for sinners, Spurgeon felt a tremendous, agonizing pastoral burden to "compel them to come in". He reasoned with sinners, warning them of the coming wrath, and pleading with them to look to the man who gave Himself for the lost. He firmly believed that winning a single soul from the pit by preaching the cross was a far more glorious achievement than being crowned a master of theological controversy or solving apocalyptic mysteries. Thus, the substitutionary atonement remained the beating heart of his monumental ministry, echoing through the thousands of sermons that reached millions of souls worldwide.
